newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban criticise UNHCR for reducing relief work.
newsitem.headline: Taleban criticise UNHCR for reducing relief work.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia on Thursday criticised the decision by the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) to put relief operations in Kabul on hold.
"We have enforced Islamic principles for the men and women of Afghanistan and the United Nations has no right to argue with them," Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters.
The UNHCR said on Wednesday it was suspending most of its programmes in Kabul in protest at what it said were arrests and intimidation of its local staff by the Taleban.
"We are putting on hold most of our programmes in Kabul until the security situation improves," said Rupert Colville, a UNHCR spokesman in the Pakistani capital, Islamabad.

He said four of the 22 local staff in the UNHCR's main office in Kabul had been arrested, while seven Afghan women employees had been told to stay at home since the Taleban militia captured Kabul on September 27.
"We are extremely concerned about the safety of our four arrested staffers, one of whom has been missing for nearly four weeks," Colville said. "The rest of our staff are petrified."
The agency says that effective security guarantees are lacking, despite assurances given by the Taleban authorities.
Mutaqi said the Taleban had instituted Islamic law in the parts of the country they control, and that if anybody had been arrested, it was for infringements of the criminal code.
He dismissed the UNHCR's reasons for cutting back its activities. "The U.N. should not seek excuses to suspend their programme," said Mutaqi.

"In general we are very happy with the activities of the U.N. Our only complaint is that they lack understanding of Afghanistan and Afghan society. We hope that they don't make the mistake of comparing Afghan society to Western society."
Mutaqi also denounced the London-based human rights agency Amnesty International, which criticised the Taleban's treatment of women and ethnic minorities in a recent report .
"The whole of the Amnesty International report is baseless." he said. "If they have proof for any of their allegations they should pass it on to the United Nations and they can judge."
Taleban-controlled Sharia radio in Kabul accused Amnesty International of interfering in internal Afghan affairs.

"Any country or organisation which deems the implementation of Islamic codes in our country a violation of human rights is acting against international norms and we consider it as interference in the internal affairs of Afghanistan," it said.

Mutaqi denied Amnesty charges that the Taleban had used prisoners to clear minefields or forced people to attend mosques. "These allegations are baseless. Amnesty International should come to Afghanistan and check for themselves," he said.
